topic.topic: The first pulsar and Jocelyn Bell
topic.angle: A scruffy bit of chart recording first nicknamed LGM-1

body.question: In 1967, grad student Jocelyn Bell spotted a "bit of scruff" on her chart recordings. The signal was pulsing. How often?
body.reveal: About one pulse every one and a third seconds. It was temporarily nicknamed "Little Green Man 1" (LGM-1), then identified as a rapidly rotating neutron star.

probes.question: True or false: Jocelyn Bell was among the recipients of the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics.

image_brief.show: Jocelyn Bell Burnell at a conference, or a radio telescope array

claims.claim: In 1967 Bell, a postgraduate student, spotted a "bit of scruff" on her chart recordings
claims.quote: while a postgraduate student at Cambridge, Bell Burnell detected a "bit of scruff" on her chart-recorder papers

claims.claim: The signal pulsed about once every one and a third seconds (answer "Every 1.3 seconds", reveal)
claims.quote: at a rate of about one pulse every one and a third seconds
claims.note: Pulsar page gives 1.337 seconds; "1.3 seconds" is that value to one decimal.

claims.claim: It was temporarily nicknamed "Little Green Man 1" (LGM-1) (reveal, probe p1)
claims.quote: Temporarily dubbed "Little Green Man 1" (LGM-1) the source

claims.claim: It was then identified as a rapidly rotating neutron star
claims.quote: was identified after several years as a rapidly rotating neutron star

claims.claim: Probe p2: Bell was NOT among the recipients of the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics (answer false)
claims.quote: This discovery was recognized by the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1974, though she was not among its recipients.
